statement: Winkte (from winyanktehca), a recognized traditional alternate/third-gender role for persons assigned male at birth, is documented (Royal B. Hassrick, The Sioux: Life and Customs of a Warrior Society, University of Oklahoma Press, 1964) as associated with women's tasks and, in some accounts, ceremonial/prophetic or matchmaking functions and elevated spiritual status. Walter L. Williams, The Spirit and the Flesh: Sexual Diversity in American Indian Culture (Beacon Press, 1986), is the foundational comparative academic synthesis treating winkte alongside Diné nádleehí as among the highest-prestige gender-variant roles documented in North America, but has been critiqued (including by Harry Hay) for conflating winkte with the modern Western category "gay" and de-emphasizing its ceremonial/spiritual dimension. Beatrice Medicine (Sihásapa/Minneconjou Lakota anthropologist), in "Directions in Gender Research in American Indian Societies: Two Spirits and Other Categories," explicitly critiques blanket use of the imported French-colonial term "berdache" for culturally distinct roles like winkte, calling for tribally-specific ethnographic contextualization rather than a single pan-Indian category. The 19th-century documentary record on winkte specifically is described in the secondary literature as genuinely sparse, with most characterization derived from later 20th-century anthropological reconstruction — an inherent source-thinness limitation on any claim about the pre-contact/19th-century role.
